analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in number 335 Oppenheimer Fund against Sanders. Mr. Berman, you may proceed, I think, whenever you're... We have some more help coming here. Whenever you're ready. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. May it please the court. Thank you. This case is a sequel to a class action litigation that preoccupied the lower courts for some eight years until it reached this court in 1974 and was the subject of a decision by this court, which is generally referred to as Eisen IV. It's officially reported in the reports as Eisen v. Carlyle and Jacqueline at 417 U.S. reports. In Eisen, this court held that Rule 23 of the Federal Civil Rules imposes an unambiguous requirement that individual notice be sent to every class member who can be identified through reasonable effort. This court further held that the cost of notice was the burden of the plaintiffs as part of the normal burden of financing their litigation. In the instant case, the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, in an en banc decision, ruled that the district court was nevertheless entitled to impose the cost of... the considerable cost of the furnishing of a list of shareholder class names at the expense of the defendants and without cost to the plaintiffs. The court of appeals, in an unambiguous requirement that the court of appeals, in this en banc decision, with three judges strongly dissenting, the court of appeals, the court of appeals, the court of appeals, the court of appeals, said it reached, it was propelled ineluctably to that determination precisely by Eisen IV itself. We think that, on the face of it, the decision of the unambiguous requirement that the decision of the unbanked majority is built on non-sequiturs, because the proportion that the court of appeals, came from the fact that this court, having held that Rule 23 requires individual notice to the members of the class, that said, for majority, that meant that the discovery proceedings of the federal rules came into full play, because it might be necessary, in some case, to deal with the contention that some class member had not received individual notice. And to do this, he had to, the court would have to have, or the parties would have to have, resort to the discovery proceedings of the federal rules, and specifically, the emphasis was placed on Rule 34, because in Rule 34, said the majority opinion, where records are computerized, the respondent may have to furnish a printout at its own cost. And there is some quotation in the advisory committee's report that, in some instances, that a printout might have to be furnished by a respondent where the records are computerized. But in this case, the record before this court shows, and that record was before the lower court, of course, there is no such printout that can be furnished. There is no such computerized record listing the members of the class. You mean a new program would have to be prepared? A new program, eight new programs would have to be prepared, specifically because there are two groups of shareholders, those who are direct shareholders, owners of the Oppenheimer Fund, and those who are members of the OSCAP plan, which periodically buys shares, and they all have a prorotic interest. And four programs would be needed for each. But it's not solely a question of the new programs, computerized programs, that would have to be prepared. The fact of the matter is that if the Second Circuit majority had felt propelled to look at the record, which you'll find in the latter part of the appendix before you, where the testimony of the transfer agent taken on deposition by Mr. Ruby of the plaintiff's counsel, it will be found that the basic documents that are needed to obtain the information that the identifying the members of the class are to be found in semi-obsolete papers in the warehouse of the transfer agent, which are in the form of ledger sheets called the Daily Journal, which in effect were transaction sheets on which were listed back in 1968 and 69, the relevant period as determined here. The transactions that took place, in other words, there's a list of purchases made and transfers made of shares of the Oppenheimer Fund on each trading day during that two-year period. And the job that has to be done, at least as to half of the class members to be determined, is for punch-key operators to sit down and punch-key cards, a card for each one of these transactions. Is there any agreement, Mr. Berman, on how much all this is going to cost? Yes, at that time, in 1973, the transfer agent came up with a price of some $16,500. And we proceed here on that premise? We, the record hasn't been altered, but I think the court may deduce... What's the value of the plaintiff's investments in Oppenheimer? The Oppenheimer Fund had assets of aggregating, at that time, some $500 million. Even the plaintiffs? I bought... Not the plaintiffs. Oh, the plaintiffs, sir. The plaintiffs had, at that time, some... some... some... 2,000 in the aggregate, some... the three plaintiffs had some 2,000 shares that had an asset value of some... a little more than that $16,000 that... How much more? I think it was in the $20,000, $20,000 range. And would that still be true today? No, it has been sharply... They have been redeeming shares over the years, and on the basis of the latest figure spreaders, they have some 800 shares in total, which would have an asset value or market value of some $5,000. That's all. That is all. I wondered, because this was a collateral order, Dr. Peel, wasn't it? Yes, that was... 1291. That is... I gather the panel found that this appeal fitted within the... The... The collateral order document. Yes, it did, Your Honor. But I... I wondered where the... where the irreparable injury was. If they had a... If they had $23,000 worth of stock and the cost involved here was $16,000, do we have a jurisdictional question on this respect to the law? Well, I wouldn't think so because they allege violations... The court and bank never reached the... They allege violations, of course, of the Investment Company Act, the Securities Act, the 10B-5, and all the usual, and therefore, they assert federal causes of action, and they're... Well, anything like that, your adversary hasn't raised any jurisdictional questions. No. Of the appeal. Not whatever. I'm speaking up to the appeal. Not whatever. Now, the... Which I guess wouldn't mean anything if we thought there was any merit to the jurisdiction. Whether or not there was jurisdiction... Now, the point I was seeking to make was that we're dealing here essentially with business records, not this series of arcane, computerized records that require secret devices to cause them to be operative and so forth, to which the majority opinion refers time and time again. And there is no reason, as a matter of fact, why they couldn't go in and perform this operation by hand if they were willing to take the burden of doing it. Was this ever presented to the district court as a discovery matter? It never was presented as a discovery matter, and in fact, the district court, in making its determination, said that this involved a question of the cost of notice to the members of the class. You never had an opportunity to make a protective order of motion under Rule 26? No, we did not, and that is one of, of course, one of the points we urge here. Any motion ever made for discovery? No, only to the extent that Mr. Ruby did move to or gave notice of his desire to take the deposition of the transfer agent with a view to determining the question of the class members and so forth. The defendant merely suggested that that be done by interrogatory rather than everybody trooping up to Boston to take the deposition, but the judge overruled that, and we all went up to Boston, and that deposition was taken, and that's the 50 pages of evidence in the back of the appendix to which I've referred you, which disclosed, as I say, that we're dealing here essentially with business records of the type that under Rule 30, even if the federal discovery rules were applicable under 33C, all that the defendant would have to do would be to make these records available to the party seeking discovery and permit him to make any cop as he wants, and even under Rule 34, Moore's federal practice confirms what every practitioner knows to be the case, that where someone wants to come in, your opponent wants to come in and see your records, you make them available, and if he says, make me copies of those, you say at your cost, of course, and he either does that or you lend them to him long enough to have them photostatted or whatever, and Moore says that that is the rule, even under 34. Now, so the only point that the majority opinion, the en banc opinion, was basing itself on was the notion that we're dealing here with computerized records and that Rule 34 is intended to give the applicant for computerized records the right to make the respondent give him a copy of his computerized, give him a printout. We have no printout to give him. Now, there are some tapes. For example, there is a current tape listing all the current shareholders of the Oppenheimer Fund at that time, 170,000 in number. Of that 170,000, 70,000 were not shareholders in the 1968-69 period, so they weren't shareholders in the relevant period. That's about 40%. Since then, that percentage has climbed, has multiplied greatly, and it's probable that two-thirds of the shareholders are not members of the class. That's the only computerized record. We don't keep a computerized record of dropout shareholders, those who've gone by the wayside. Perhaps we should, like some institutions of higher earning, have a list of alumni who are frequently circularized, might be a good idea. It hasn't been done. So that we have to go back to those transactions sheets in 1968 and 69 and laboriously compile those 300,000 cards by this key punch operation. and then from those cards make tapes which combined with existing tapes and various programs, eight in number, would ultimately produce a list of the class members as it was as of 1968 and 69 and that would entail this cost. And we're perfectly willing to cooperate in every way. We've made, we've offered to have them see the records. We did not oppose their taking the deposition of the transfer agent. But why should we be obliged to go and pay for it? Now, of course, you could take judicial notice of what's happened to the trend of prices in the last five years. It goes without saying that the cost is very much higher today. In fact, double, I would say. And at the same time, what has happened is, and the record shows that the start had already been made. There was a wave of redemptions going on. That is, shareholders have the right to come in and tender their shares to the management to receive their money. The market had gone down in 1973, the time when this class action motion was made. And there was a wave of redemptions which we were fearful would be further instigated if the class action letter went to the 70,000 members who weren't their class members but mere shareholders of the fund. Now, that trend has continued and to the point where today, I wish to, that 43 million shares of the then 67 million have been the subject of redemptions over the intervening years so that it is probable that now two-thirds of the current shareholders are not class members. And simultaneously, the cost of locating the records for those who have dropped out again will continue to pile up. Mr. Berman, perhaps the briefs tell and I don't remember, but how was the class period defined the dates? What gave rise to this election? The plaintiffs allege that when they purchased shares, very modest amounts of shares in 1968 and 69, that they were not given, they were either given no information about the so-called restricted securities that the fund had commenced to purchase in 1968 or when they did get information, it didn't correctly set forth how that the value of those securities was determined for a purpose of determining the total assets of the fund on the basis of which the selling price of the shares is determined, that is, they're sold to them at net asset value per share for a servicing charge. Is the 68th date then the date of the first purchases of restricted securities? In 68, the first report emerged in which there was some reference to these restricted securities and that was amplified further and the district judge said he thought that, and we actually, the fund, suggested that the relevant period be limited to the year 1968 so as to narrow the cost to everybody involved in the bar. But the district judge said no because the prospectus for 1970 gave more information than was given in the 1969 prospectus, so he thought he'd better leave it at that two years, 68, 69, as the relevant period. And that's the way it was. Now, all this emphasis on these restricted securities and non-disclosure, the alleged non-disclosure, leave out of account the fact that there was nothing arcane or secret or unusual about purchase by investment companies of these so-called restricted securities. And of course, I believe you all realize that what is meant by restricted securities is that they are securities not yet the subject of a registration statement which has become effective under the Securities Act of 33. So a public offering cannot at that point be made, but each purchase was accompanied by an undertaking of the seller, of the selling company, the issuer company, that it would register these securities with the SEC on demand or at a certain time and most of them then that was carried out in due course. But in the meantime, of course, they were not saleable to the public as freely as the others. There were places they couldn't sell. What you're telling us now goes to the merits of this litigation. Yes, it does. Not to the issue now before us. Precisely. But I do want to point out and we cite in our brief that the Securities and Exchange Commission itself said that as of the end of 1968, the mutual fund industry owned four and a quarter billion dollars of these restricted securities. securities. They were in great demand and the public was very interested in them to the point where a fund was launched in 1968 and we cite that again and raised 55 million dollars for investment predominantly in these restricted securities and it was a great success. I mean, on the selling end and so forth. Now, our opponent here has made a big point in his brief about the special the special fiduciary obligations of directors and officers and affiliates of mutual funds. They are indeed under special fiduciary obligations. Did the Court of Appeals pass on that point in the in-bank opinion? No, they did not. It had been made, that point had been made by Judge Hayes as a member of the three-judge panel. The dissenting member of the three-judge panel. When it came to the opinion of the en-bank court, that was not touched on at all as the dissenters pointed out. We'll resume there at 10 o'clock in the morning, Mr. Vermin.
